newsitem.title: USA: Postal Service wins battle, but war rage on.
newsitem.headline: Postal Service wins battle, but war rage on.

text.p: The market war over express mail could heat up further following a key ruling this week from an advertising industry regulatory board that upheld the U.S. Postal Service's high-profile competitive ad campaign.
The National Advertising Review Board, the industry's highest self-regulatory body, reversed an earlier staff ruling that said the comparative ads were misleading.
But Federal Express is still challenging the ads in U.S. District Court in Memphis, and it is forging ahead with a campaign of its own that challenges the Postal Service's truthfulness.

The tussle began in March when the U.S. Postal Service launched an ad campaign for its Priority Mail service in which it compared the price of its express service with that of Federal Express and UPS. The ads, by True North's Foote, Cone & Belding, tout its much cheaper price but leave out other details that distinguish the products' services, such as delivery guarantees and tracking capabilities.

"It's an apples-to-oranges comparison," said Ira Bahr, senior vice president and worldwide account director at FedEx's ad agency, BBDO Worldwide in New York. "Priority Mail is not guaranteed, not tracked. Customers don't know when it's going to arrive. If there is a price difference between the Postal Service and its competitors, it is because they are not the same product."

Determined to set the record straight, Federal Express launched a national radio ad campaign last fall using biting humour to drive home the ads' point: "For reliable, two-day service, no one makes your package a priority like FedEx"

In one spot, a customer seeks delivery of his package on a Saturday. A double-talking postal clerk tells him, "You might get it friend. And if it gets there, you pay nothing extra," he chirps. "And if it doesn't?" the customer asks. "You pay nothing extra, lucky man."

The Priority Mail campaign earlier caught the attention of the National Advertising Division of the Council of Better Business Bureaus, which in November concluded that the Postal Service needed to change its ads to disclose that Priority Mail is not tracked or guaranteed.

The Postal Service appealed the decision to the National Advertising Review Board, which led to the reversal of the board's decision and left the Postal Service free to continue with its comparative ads.
"We feel we're on a firm ground to go forward," said Jeff Tarakajian, senior vice president and group management director for Foote, Cone & Belding.
FedEx said in a statement after the ruling that it "strongly disagreed" with the panel's decision.
"Consumers have told us they have been misled by the Postal Service ads," the company said. "We are attempting to give the public the facts through our radio campaign."

Already, the Postal Service has spent $55 million on the Priority Mail campaign alone. Given the Postal Service's okay to continue its comparative campaign, and FedEx's response, an advertising war could just be heating up.
But regardless of who wins the argument, consumers already have profited. On Nov. 1, FedEx lowered the cost of its second-day delivery services by 35 percent.
"Priority Mail has proven itself. FedEx has reduced prices. What could be better for consumers?" said Tarakajian of Foote, Cone.
